The abstract and p10 report 100% negative SMDs and p = 0.003 for temperature on postexercise glycogen content, but the review's own p10 sentence garbles the direction ('decreases glycogen utilization'). The brief's reading of lower glycogen in heat matches the included studies ('Muscle glycogenolysis is increased in the heat') and the authors' conclusion, so it is defensible, though the sign is not spelled out unambiguously in the source.

p5-6 match, including the authors' equipment caveat.

statementIssues.note: Imperative phrasing ('Start carbohydrate and protein early after the lift', 'Rehydrate actively ...') reads close to a directive at the Limited tier. The content is consistent across C1/C8/C23/C6 and recommendedDirection is null, but options or conditional wording would fit the tier better.

Option C ties 'smaller amounts' for GI tolerance to the Ivy 1988 glycogen dose study. The brief transparently says that study measured glycogen, not GI symptoms, so the GI rationale is professional inference rather than evidence.
'A separate UEFA statement on Ramadan fasting' is the Ramadan section of the same UEFA expert group statement (p12), not a separate document.

The 2%-6% CHO beverage and chilled-drink sentences carry no supporting claim after C31 was removed. They are accurate to UEFA p11 ('When rehydration is the priority, ingesting a 2%-6% CHO beverage may be of greater benefit ...'; 'providing chilled beverages will promote voluntary fluid intake') but are untraceable in the brief.

The UEFA 'less than about 2% to 3%' body mass loss figure is accurate (p4, p11) but uncited after a claim reference was dropped. The urine color/USG statement omits the authors' caveat that few athletes reached 2% BML.

'heat significantly lowered post-exercise muscle glycogen' inherits C35's direction ambiguity and reads causally for a pooled analysis of 4 small crossover studies with heterogeneity (I2 = 67%) and a prediction interval crossing zero.

tierNote: Limited is appropriate. No source tests a lift followed by field practice. GI evidence is review, consensus or a cited cyclist study. Numeric targets come from a narrative RL review and match-day consensus guidance, and the hydration-glycogen evidence is in tension. No Recommended Direction was given, and actions are framed as options with labeled professional judgment.
usefulnessNote: A sports dietitian or performance staffer gets the practical building blocks for a 4-6 hour gap: post-lift CHO/protein timing and amounts, rehydration volume and sodium, daily CHO ranges, pre-practice and during-practice options, and GI-tolerance strategies. Each comes with honest notes on transferability (RL, match-day, cyclist data). The coverage gaps are specific. It is long for a two-minute read, and some uncited UEFA content remains after claim removal.
suggestedDrafterFixes: When the verifier removes a claim, also remove or rewrite every statement sentence that depended only on that claim, instead of only dropping the claim reference, so no uncited factual content survives.
At Limited or Coverage Gap tiers, constrain bottomLine wording to descriptive or conditional phrasing (for example 'sources support early post-exercise carbohydrate') rather than imperatives.
When citing different sections of one source, name the section ('the Ramadan section of the same UEFA statement') rather than implying a separate document.
For meta-analysis claims, state the outcome direction from the included studies' conclusions and add heterogeneity/prediction-interval caveats when the source reports them.
Cap action text length or add a one-line summary per action so the brief can be read in about two minutes.
